stem: A coil is connected to a sensitive meter. When is a current induced in the coil?

options.content: While a magnet is moving into or out of it
While a magnet rests inside it
When the coil is near a stationary magnet
Never: coils cannot produce current

explanation: A current is induced only while the magnetic field through the coil is changing, for example while a magnet moves in or out.

stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil and a centre-zero meter flicks to the right. The magnet is then pulled out at the same speed. What does the meter do?

options.content: It flicks to the left.
It flicks to the right again.
It does not move.
It flicks further to the right.

explanation: Pulling the magnet out reverses the change, so the induced current, and the deflection, reverse.

stem: A strong magnet held still inside a coil induces a steady current in the coil.
explanation: With no relative motion the field through the coil does not change, so no e.m.f. is induced.

stem: Select **all** the changes that increase the size of the induced e.m.f. when a magnet is pushed into a coil.

options.content: Turning the magnet round
options.rationale: This reverses the e.m.f. without increasing it.

options.content: Using a coil with more turns
Using a stronger magnet
Holding the magnet still inside the coil
Moving the magnet more slowly
Moving the magnet faster

explanation: Faster motion, a stronger magnet and more turns all increase the induced e.m.f.
hints: Which changes make the field through the coil change faster or more?

stem: A straight wire is moved along the direction of the magnetic field lines between the poles of a magnet. What is induced in it?

options.content: No e.m.f., because the wire cuts no field lines
The largest e.m.f., as it moves along the field
options.rationale: That needs motion across the field.

options.content: An alternating e.m.f. that changes direction
options.rationale: There is no e.m.f. at all without cutting field lines.

options.content: A small steady current along the wire
options.rationale: No field lines are cut, so nothing is induced.

explanation: An e.m.f. is induced only when the wire cuts across field lines.

options.content: The induced current always helps the change producing it.
options.rationale: That would create energy from nothing.

options.content: The induced current always opposes the change producing it.
The induced current always flows clockwise in a coil.
options.rationale: Its direction depends on the change.

options.content: The induced e.m.f. always equals the battery e.m.f.
options.rationale: A battery is not needed for induction.

explanation: Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. and current oppose the change that causes them.

stem: The north pole of a magnet is pushed towards one end of a coil that is part of a closed circuit. Which pole is induced at that end of the coil?

options.content: A south pole, which attracts the magnet
options.rationale: That would help the motion, not oppose it.

options.content: A north pole, which repels the approaching magnet
No pole, because the coil is not a permanent magnet
options.rationale: The induced current makes the coil a magnet.

options.content: A north pole, which attracts the magnet

explanation: To oppose the approach of a north pole, the near end of the coil becomes a north pole and repels it.
hints: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change.

stem: The south pole of a magnet is pulled away from one end of a coil in a closed circuit. Which pole forms at that end of the coil?

options.content: A south pole, which repels the magnet as it leaves
options.rationale: That would help it move away.

options.content: No pole, because the magnet is moving away from that end of it
A north pole, attracting the magnet to oppose its removal
A south pole, which attracts the magnet

explanation: The change is a south pole moving away; to oppose it, the coil end becomes a north pole and pulls the magnet back.
hints: The induced pole must try to stop the magnet leaving.

stem: Lenz's law is a consequence of which principle?

options.content: Conservation of charge
Newton's first law
Ohm's law
Conservation of energy
options.rationale: Correct: work must be done against the opposing force.

explanation: Because the induced current opposes the motion, work must be done to move the magnet, and that work becomes electrical energy.
hints: What would happen if the induced current helped the magnet move?

stem: A horizontal wire is moved upwards between a north pole on the left and a south pole on the right. Which way does the induced current flow in the wire?

options.content: Out of the page
To the left
options.rationale: The current is along the wire, at right angles to the field and motion.

options.content: Into the page
To the right

explanation: Right hand: thumb up (motion), first finger to the right (field): the second finger points into the page.
hints: Use Fleming's right-hand rule: thuMb motion, First finger field, seCond finger current.

stem: In Fleming's right-hand rule, what does the thumb represent?

options.content: The magnetic field
The induced current
The force on the current
The motion of the conductor

explanation: Right-hand rule: thuMb Motion, First finger Field, seCond finger induced Current.

payload.template: An e.m.f. is induced only when there is relative {{blank:a}} between a conductor and a magnetic field, or when the field linking a coil {{blank:b}}.

explanation: Induction needs relative motion that cuts field lines, or a changing field.

stem: A learner has a coil of wire, a bar magnet and a sensitive centre-zero meter.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe an experiment to show electromagnetic induction, and what is observed.

points.description: Connect the coil to the meter and push the magnet into the coil: the needle deflects
Hold the magnet still: no deflection; pull it out: the needle deflects the opposite way
Move the magnet faster: the deflection is larger

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why is a centre-zero meter used?

options.content: It can measure very large currents.
It never needs zeroing before use.
The induced current flows either way; the needle shows both.
It works only with a.c., which is the only kind of induced current
options.rationale: It shows d.c. in either direction.

parts.explanation: The current reverses between pushing in and pulling out, so the needle must be able to move either way.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: The magnet is replaced by a stronger one, moved at the same speed. What happens to the deflection?

options.content: It is smaller.
It is larger.
It is the same.
options.rationale: A stronger field gives a larger e.m.f.

options.content: It reverses.
options.rationale: Only the direction of motion or the pole reverses it.

parts.explanation: A stronger magnet gives a faster change of field, so a larger e.m.f.

explanation: Relative motion induces an e.m.f.; its direction depends on the direction of motion, its size on speed, field strength and turns.
hints: Think about pushing in, holding still and pulling out.
